newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia peacekeepers hunt for arms after deadline.
newsitem.headline: Liberia peacekeepers hunt for arms after deadline.

text.p: West African peacekeepers began hunting for arms in Liberia's capital Monrovia on Saturday, vowing to crack down on faction fighters found with weapons after the expiry of a disarmament deadline.
But General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led force, said fighters in remote areas outside Monrovia had an extra seven days to disarm voluntarily.
"After that, we will start conducting military operations and we will not allow anyone to stand in our way," he told a news conference. "We will go for the arms where ever they are in Liberia."
The disarmament deadline, part of a peace deal envisaging elections in May to end seven years of civil war, expired at midnight on Friday. The exercise began on November 22.
Malu said that 23,403 fighters had disarmed out of an estimated total of 30-35,000. He described earlier estimates of up to 60,000 fighters as unrealistic.
Several thousand child soldiers and women were among those who disarmed.
Freed American slaves founded Liberia in 1847.

The fighters have held the shattered West African nation hostage during seven years of civil war, in which well over 150,000 people have been killed. Hundreds of people died in the capital in an orgy of looting and fighting in April and May.
Fighters queued on Friday in Monrovia and at over a dozen centres around the West African nation to swap their weapons for land, food or educational vouchers ahead of the deadline.

Malu said mobile teams of peacekeepers would take weapons from fighters in remote areas who chose to surrender them but that searches in Monrovia would begin immediately. "The house to house searches in Monrovia will continue and in other areas where elections are expected to take place," he said.
Earlier, peacekeepers with tanks and armoured personnel carriers deployed in parts of Monrovia, hunting for weapons.
"We will deal with anyone found with arms (of war) in Liberia," ECOMOG chief-of-staff Brigadier General Abdul-One Mohammed told reporters in Liberia's Royesville township.

He said that fighters spotted with arms in the township on Friday had disappeared into the surrounding forest but had left behind a cache of arms in a gutted church. They included automatic rifles and grenade launchers.
Malu has repeatedly said that fighters keeping weapons beyond the deadline would be treated as criminals.

West African leaders, who brokered the peace deal in Nigeria's capital Abuja in August, have threatened individual sanctions against anyone derailing the process. Over a dozen earlier deals collapsed.
Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war, and Alhaji Kromah, his sometime rival but his ally against ethnic Krahn factions in April and May, say they plan to run for president.
Their Krahn rival Roosevelt Johnson has said he plans to go into business rather than politics.
The war pitted the descendants of the slaves, grouped with indigenous allies within Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia, against the Krahn who supplanted them in the 1980s and their allies.
Malu also said that the curfew had been eased and would run from midnight to 5.30 a.m. instead of 10 p.m. to 6 a.m..
